beginner: The economy grew 2.2% last year, which is solid but not booming, meaning businesses are hiring slowly and consumers aren't spending like they did during the pandemic rush.
Growth at 2.2% sits right in the sweet spot the Fed wants, where inflation stays under control without pushing unemployment higher.
At 2.2%, the economy has room to accelerate before the Fed worries about overheating, but it also means wage pressure stays modest.
moderate: 2.2% growth arrived while the Fed holds rates at 3.25% and inflation ticked to 2.4% in February, suggesting the soft landing playbook remains on track.
This pace matches the long-term trend growth economists estimate for the US, so there's no excess slack appearing in the labor market yet.
Watch whether the 2.2% rate holds or dips when Q1 2026 data arrives, because any slowdown below 2% would force the Fed to consider cuts before December.
expert: 2.2% YoY growth with the yield curve at +73bps and unemployment stable at 4.2% confirms the economy is neither overheating nor stalling as of late Q1.
Fed guidance pegs neutral rate between 2.5% and 3.5%, meaning 3.25% policy rate leaves modest real tightness, which aligns with 2.2% growth without deflation risk.
If Q1 GDP prints below 2.0%, the market will price in rate cuts before December despite inflation at 2.3%, so March CPI on April 10 becomes the pivot point.

beginner: Inflation rose to 2.4% in February after jumping from January, and the Fed is watching closely because prices stopped cooling.
The 2.4% reading sits just above the Fed's 2% target, so the central bank is holding rates steady to make sure inflation doesn't creep higher.
When March CPI comes out April 10, if it stays near 2.4%, the Fed will likely wait until December before cutting rates.
moderate: February's 0.3% monthly gain (up from 0.2% in January) pushed the annual rate to 2.4%, signaling disinflation has stalled after months of steady declines from the 2022 peak.
The 2.3% current figure sits where the Fed expected inflation to land by mid-2026, so the recent acceleration raises questions about whether wage growth or energy prices are re-igniting pressure.
The Fed's hold-steady guidance through December makes sense only if March CPI moderates back toward 2.1%, otherwise the market will reprice rate-cut odds downward.
expert: CPI at 2.3% with a +0.3% monthly print in February and the 10Y yield at 4.34% implies the market is pricing in stickiness above the Fed's target through mid-2026.
Real Fed funds rate sits at +0.95% (3.25% minus 2.3% inflation), which is restrictive but not punishing, allowing 2.2% growth without demand collapse.
March CPI on April 10 will determine whether the Fed can credibly maintain its December-first-cut messaging or must signal extended pause, with market pricing shifting at any reading above 2.5% YoY.

beginner: The jobless rate sits at 4.2%, which is low enough that workers have bargaining power but high enough that the Fed isn't panicked about overheating.
At 4.2%, there's still slack in the labor market, meaning companies aren't desperate to hire and wages aren't spiraling out of control.
The Fed watches unemployment closely because if it drops much below 4%, wage pressure typically rises and pushes inflation higher.
moderate: Unemployment at 4.2% has held steady even as GDP grew only 2.2%, which suggests companies are hoarding labor rather than laying off, a sign of caution.
This level is near the Fed's estimate of the natural rate (around 4.1% to 4.3%), so there's little room for the jobless rate to fall without triggering wage acceleration.
If unemployment ticks up to 4.5% or higher in the next few months, the Fed will have cover to cut rates even if inflation stays above 2%.
expert: 4.2% unemployment with 2.2% growth and inflation at 2.3% places the economy in the Fed's estimated neutral zone, where the output gap is near zero.
Real wage growth has turned positive recently in most data, which at 4.2% jobless suggests the Phillips curve remains flat and wage-price spirals are contained.
A rise to 4.5% unemployment would shift Fed messaging toward easing before December, but any drop below 4.0% with inflation holding above 2.3% forces the hold-tight scenario.

beginner: The US government is spending 6.9% more than it takes in each year, a massive hole that Washington keeps digging even as the economy grows.
This 6.9% deficit means the Treasury borrows hundreds of billions monthly, competing with private businesses for investors' money and driving up interest rates.
Over time, huge deficits like this force the government to cut spending or raise taxes, but neither happens easily in an election year.
moderate: At 6.9% of GDP, the deficit is near its post-pandemic peak and well above the pre-crisis average of 2% to 3%, driven by entitlements and defense spending neither party wants to cut.
The Treasury's need to borrow aggressively pushes up the 10Y yield to 4.34%, crowding out private investment and making it harder for companies to fund expansion.
If the deficit stays above 6% through 2026, the Fed will face pressure to raise rates to attract foreign buyers of Treasuries, offsetting any inflation disinflation.
expert: Budget deficit at 6.9% GDP with 10Y yield at 4.34% and the Treasury's rollover needs accelerating creates a fiscal-monetary policy tension the market will exploit if long yields spike.
Structural deficit (adjusted for the cycle) exceeds 5%, meaning even if the economy were at full capacity, Washington would still borrow unsustainably.
If the 10Y breaches 4.75% within 12 months due to fiscal concerns, the Fed's December rate-cut scenario evaporates and markets retest the -3.6% YTD decline in equities.

beginner: America imports far more than it exports, running a deficit of 3.7% of GDP, which means the country as a whole spends more abroad than it earns.
This trade gap is mostly financed by foreign investors buying US assets, so dollars flow back into Treasury bonds and stocks instead of real goods.
A 3.7% current account deficit is large but normal for the US, reflecting that America is attractive to global capital.
moderate: The 3.7% current account deficit has widened from the pandemic low of 2.5% as consumer demand rebounded faster than US exports, a typical post-recession pattern.
This deficit is financed by a capital account surplus (foreigners buying US stocks, bonds, and real estate), which works only as long as foreign investors trust US assets.
If the USD weakens below 97 on the DXY (it's at 98.8 now), the current account may narrow as imports become expensive, but that takes time to show in trade data.
expert: Current account at 3.7% GDP deficit with USD/DXY at 98.8 and 10Y yields at 4.34% implies foreign central banks and private investors are still willing to finance the US external position despite fiscal imbalance.

The deficit reflects both structural factors (high US productivity and capital demand) and cyclical factors (strong consumption post-pandemic), so expect it to stabilize between 3.2% and 4.0% through 2026.
Watch for any sharp dollar weakening below 97 DXY, which would signal loss of foreign demand for US assets and force either higher yields or lower growth to rebalance the external position.

beginner: The Fed is holding its main interest rate at 3.25% and plans to keep it there until December, betting that inflation will stay under control without any rate cuts.
At 3.25%, borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans, and credit cards are sticky high, which slows spending and keeps the economy from overheating.
If inflation cools faster than expected, the Fed might cut rates earlier, but the March CPI on April 10 is the key test.
moderate: The Fed's hold-through-December stance assumes inflation moderates from 2.4% in February back toward 2%, allowing rates to stay restrictive without crushing growth.
At 3.25%, the real policy rate is +0.95% (after subtracting 2.3% inflation), which is still restrictive enough to cool demand but not so tight as to trigger recession risk.
If March CPI accelerates above 2.5% or unemployment drops below 4.0%, the Fed will extend the hold into Q1 2027, flattening the yield curve further.
expert: 3.25% policy rate with forward guidance pinning first cut to December implies the Fed's terminal-rate expectation has shifted downward from the 4.0% neutral estimate made in 2023.
Real rate of +0.95% is neutral to slightly restrictive by modern standards, consistent with 2.2% growth and 2.3% inflation, but any acceleration in either metric forces recalibration.

Market pricing as of April 8 likely embeds 50 to 75bps of cuts through December; if the May jobs report or Q1 GDP surprise to the downside, the first cut moves to June and the entire curve reprices lower.

beginner: The stock market is down 3.6% so far in 2026, erasing some of the gains from late 2025 as investors worry about slowing growth and sticky inflation.
A 3.6% decline is not a crash, just a correction, and it's typical when the Fed stays patient and bond yields stay elevated.
If the economy slows more or inflation accelerates further, stocks could fall another 5% to 10%, but the underlying corporate earnings are still solid.
moderate: Stocks are down 3.6% YTD while the 10Y yield climbed to 4.34%, a classic rotation away from growth stocks toward bonds that offer safer returns.
This decline is concentrated in expensive mega-cap tech names that thrive on low rates; value and dividend stocks are holding up better as investors chase yield.
If the Fed cuts rates in December as expected, the market typically rebounds 10% to 15% in the months before and after, so the current dip is likely a buying opportunity for patient investors.
expert: Equities down 3.6% YTD with 10Y at 4.34%, USD/DXY at 98.8, and earnings revisions neutral to slightly negative reflect a repricing of growth assumptions from 2.5% to 2.0% in the consensus.

The -3.6% YTD decline is proportional to the 73bps yield curve steepening and the market's 25% probability shift of no-cut scenario in 2026, implying fair value is 8% to 12% lower if real rates stay above 1.0%.
Key catalysts: If March CPI moderates below 2.2% or April jobs growth falls below 150k, expect a 5% to 7% rally into May; if either surprises higher, -3.6% YTD becomes -8% to -10% by June.

beginner: The 10-year Treasury yield is 4.34%, which sets the baseline for mortgage rates, corporate bond costs, and what investors demand to lend money safely for a decade.
At 4.34%, borrowing costs are high enough that companies and homebuyers think twice before taking on debt, which slows economic growth a bit.
If the Fed cuts rates in December, the 10Y yield will likely fall to 3.8% to 4.0%, making mortgages and business loans cheaper.
moderate: The 10Y yield at 4.34% reflects both the Fed's 3.25% rate and a 109bps term premium, which is elevated relative to the historical 70bps average, signaling caution about long-term growth.
This level is above the rough neutral rate of 4.0% to 4.25%, so it's pricing in fiscal concerns (6.9% deficit) and uncertainty about the Fed's path beyond December.
If inflation re-accelerates to 2.6% or higher, the 10Y could spike to 4.75%, inverting the crude expectations for December cuts and forcing the Fed to hold longer.
expert: 10Y at 4.34% with real yield near 2.1% (4.34% minus 2.3% inflation) is on the elevated side of the Fed's estimated neutral range of 1.7% to 2.2%, signaling lingering inflation expectations or term-premium compression risk.

The 73bps yield curve steepening (10Y at 4.34% minus 2Y near 3.61%) is consistent with market pricing of three to four 25bps cuts starting in December, but that compresses if Q1 GDP disappoints or March CPI surprises higher.

Watch for 10Y breakout above 4.55% as a signal that foreign buyers are retreating from Treasuries due to fiscal concerns or higher global rates, which would force the Fed into a policy dilemma (cut into weakness or hold and watch growth crater).

beginner: The yield curve is 73 basis points steep (the 10Y yield is 73 points higher than the 2Y), which is a healthy sign that investors trust the economy will keep growing.
A steep curve usually means the economy is recovering and job growth is steady, so companies are confident enough to borrow and invest.
If the curve flattens back below 50 basis points, it signals recession worry, but at 73 basis points, the market is still fairly optimistic.
moderate: The 73bps steepness is a complete reversal from the inverted yield curve of 2022 to 2023, reflecting the market's shift from recession fears to soft-landing expectations.
This steepness is fueled by expectations of Fed cuts starting in December, which pushes down the 2Y yield while the 10Y stays sticky due to fiscal and inflation concerns.
If the Fed maintains rates above 3.25% through Q1 2027 instead of cutting in December, the curve will flatten sharply as the market reprices, potentially compressing below 40bps.
expert: Yield curve at +73bps with a 10Y at 4.34% and implied December cut pricing of 75bps reflects a market consensus of two-to-three 25bps cuts in late 2026 followed by hold into mid-2027.
The steepness is supported by real rate normalization (real 10Y near 2.1% is neutral, real 2Y near 1.3% is slightly restrictive), creating space for cuts without signaling panic.
Inversion risk emerges only if March CPI surprises above 2.6% or Q1 GDP falls below 1.5%; in either case, the curve flattens to +30 to +50bps within eight weeks as cut expectations vanish.

beginner: The US dollar is trading at 98.8 on the strength index, meaning it's still strong against other major currencies even though US interest rates are no longer the highest globally.
A strong dollar makes US exports more expensive abroad but makes imports cheaper, which is part of why America runs a large trade deficit.
If the Fed cuts rates in December as expected, the dollar could weaken to 96 to 97, which would help exporters but make foreign vacations more expensive for Americans.
moderate: USD/DXY at 98.8 is down from the 2022 peak of 114 but still above the pre-pandemic average of 95 to 97, reflecting that the Fed is holding rates higher than most other central banks.
This level is sustainable as long as the 10Y yield stays above 4.25% and real yields outpace Europe and Japan, but any combination of Fed cuts and slower growth will weaken it further.
If the dollar weakens to 95 DXY, the current account deficit begins to shrink as imports become expensive, a natural rebalancing that takes 6 to 9 months to show in trade data.
expert: USD/DXY at 98.8 reflects a 2.1% real yield on the 10Y (4.34% minus 2.3% inflation) that is attractive to foreign buyers despite budget deficit concerns and slower 2.2% growth.
The Fed's expected December cuts will compress the dollar to 96 to 97 DXY, a move already partially priced in by 75bps of forward rate cuts the market is betting on.

Key pivot: If the March CPI surprises above 2.5% and the Fed delays its first cut to March 2027, the dollar rallies back above 100 DXY within six weeks, hurting multinationals' earnings translation and widening the current account deficit even further.

beginner: The stock market is down 3.12% in USD terms so far in 2026, which is a smaller loss than the 3.6% headline decline because the strong dollar is helping foreign investors get more value when they convert back home.
For a US investor, the 3.6% loss is what matters, but for a European or Japanese investor, the weaker euro or yen means they've lost even less of their purchasing power.
As the dollar weakens (if the Fed cuts rates), foreign investors will see bigger gains when they convert back to their own currency, which could attract more buying.
moderate: The 3.12% USD-adjusted decline versus 3.6% headline reflects a 48bps currency headwind (the dollar gained 0.5% of purchasing power relative to trading partners), which typically alleviates as the Fed moves toward cuts.
This currency adjustment matters for earnings estimates, as multinational corporations with large overseas revenue see dollar strength reduce reported profits by 1% to 2% in consolidated financials.
If the Fed cuts 75bps by year-end and the dollar weakens to 96 DXY, the currency tailwind reverses, boosting reported earnings by 2% to 3% and potentially lifting the market 5% to 8% by December.
expert: Stock returns at -3.12% USD-adjusted versus -3.6% headline reflect USD/DXY at 98.8 providing a currency buffer, but this advantage evaporates as Fed rate-cut expectations re-price lower (75bps cut currently priced, but March CPI will test that).

The 48bps currency tailwind is embedded in forward guidance; if the Fed holds through Q1 2027, the dollar rallies to 101 DXY, flipping the currency impact to a 80 to 100bps annual headwind on foreign revenue.

Watch the May ECB decision and BoJ April guidance; if either signals tighter policy than expected, the dollar strengthens, compressing US equity valuations by 2% to 4% in real terms even if earnings hold steady.

beginner: Inflation ticked up in February to 2.4%, the fastest pace in months, which means the Fed's plan to keep interest rates on hold through December is now under pressure.
The March CPI report drops tomorrow (April 10) and could force the Fed to reconsider whether waiting until December is still the right call.
This matters because higher inflation erodes purchasing power for workers, and if the trend continues, borrowing costs could rise sooner than expected.
moderate: CPI accelerated to 2.4% in February after tracking 2.1% in December, a clear reversal of the disinflationary trend that dominated late 2025, and March data tomorrow will signal whether this is momentum or noise.

The Fed's hold-steady guidance through December now looks vulnerable if momentum persists, a sharp contrast to the rate-cut environment most of last year when inflation was perceived as under control.

Unemployment sits at 4.4%, above the 4.2% full-year forecast, suggesting the labor market is cooling just as price pressure re-emerges, a combination that leaves little room for rate cuts and raises recession risk if growth slows further.
expert: Core CPI momentum has reversed: February's 0.3% print (2.4% annualized) breaks the disinflationary tail from Q4 2025, and the March release on April 10 will determine if the Fed's December hold is credible or a policy error in waiting.

The Fed funds rate sits at 3.64%, 41 basis points above forecast equilibrium (3.25%), and with unemployment at 4.4% (20 bps above the 4.2% forecast), the policy stance has tightened in real terms as inflation re-accelerates.

Forward signal: a March print above 2.5% annualized could force Fed communication to shift toward optionality (hikes or extended holds) well before December, collapsing the certainty premium priced into long-dated bonds and widening term spreads.

fxRegime.label: Free Float
fxRegime.beginner: The US dollar floats freely - its value is set by supply and demand in global markets. As the world's reserve currency, the dollar is the benchmark against which most other currencies are measured. The DXY index shown here is not a single exchange rate - it measures the dollar's strength against a basket of 6 major currencies (euro, yen, pound, Canadian dollar, Swedish krona, Swiss franc). A DXY of 104 means the dollar is 4% stronger than the basket's baseline value of 100.
fxRegime.moderate: Free float. The dollar's value is market-determined with no intervention target. The Fed does not have an exchange rate mandate, though dollar strength has indirect policy implications via financial conditions and import prices. The DXY index measures USD against a basket of 6 major currencies.
fxRegime.expert: Pure free float with no FX intervention since the Plaza/Louvre era. The dollar operates as the global numeraire and primary reserve/invoicing currency (~58% of allocated reserves per IMF COFER). Treasury's Exchange Stabilization Fund exists but is dormant. Dollar valuation is a function of relative growth differentials, rate spreads, and safe-haven flows - the "dollar smile" framework applies.

GDP Growth.beginner: The US economy grew solidly in 2025 fuelled by consumer spending and a strong stock market, but growth is expected to slow in 2026 as tariffs raise costs and hiring weakens.
GDP Growth.moderate: US GDP growth is forecast at 2.6% for 2026 (above consensus), driven by OBBBA tax cuts and easier financial conditions, but tariff drag and a deteriorating labour market (unemployment trending toward 4.4%) pose meaningful downside risk.
GDP Growth.expert: Goldman forecasts US real GDP at 2.6% for 2026, outperforming consensus by 0.6pp on the strength of the OBBBA fiscal impulse and reduced tariff drag post-SCOTUS IEEPA ruling; the Iran oil shock introduces a stagflationary supply-side headwind that could compress the growth rate by 0.3-0.5pp if Brent stays above $90 through Q2.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: US prices rose 2.4% in January compared to a year earlier, still above the Fed's 2% target, and the jump in oil prices from the Middle East conflict could push inflation higher again in the coming months.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: US CPI was 2.4% in January (ex-shutdown distortions ~2.7%), with tariff passthrough expected to add 0.3pp in H1 2026; the Iran energy shock could add a further 0.5-1.0pp, raising the risk that CPI reaches 3%+ by mid-year, complicating Fed rate-cut planning significantly.
Inflation (CPI).expert: US PCE inflation (the Fed's preferred gauge) ran at approximately 2.6% entering 2026; tariff-driven goods CPI uplift (+1.3-1.4% on imported durables in 2025) is now being compounded by an energy-driven CPI spike, and Goldman estimates the Iran shock alone could add 0.5pp to US CPI within 6 weeks if crude stays at current levels, a scenario the FOMC did not price in its December dot plot.

Unemployment.beginner: About 130,000 new jobs were created in January, fewer than expected, and the unemployment rate has risen to 4.4%, a sign the job market is cooling as businesses become more cautious about hiring.
Unemployment.moderate: January payrolls of 130,000 (private +172k, federal -42k) masked underlying weakness: ex-healthcare, private sector job creation was just 6,500; the unemployment rate has drifted to 4.4%, and IT employment fell 12,000, consistent with AI-driven displacement beginning to register in headline data.
Unemployment.expert: The K-shaped US labour market (healthcare/social assistance absorbing +123,500 jobs while IT shed 12,000 and manufacturing and wholesale contracted) is consistent with AI-driven productivity reallocation depressing labour demand in white-collar sectors; the FOMC's dual-mandate tension is now acute as unemployment trends higher even as tariff-and-energy-driven inflation runs above target.

Budget Deficit.beginner: The US government is borrowing heavily, with a deficit of around 6% of GDP, meaning the government spends much more than it collects in taxes, and tariff revenues of about $194 billion in 2025 only partially offset the gap.
Budget Deficit.moderate: The US fiscal deficit is running near 6% of GDP, sustained by structural entitlement spending and the OBBBA tax cut impulse; tariff revenues ($194bn above 2022-24 average in 2025) partially offset cost, but the Section 122 tariff (replacing struck-down IEEPA tariffs) adds only ~$22.3bn annually, leaving a structurally wide deficit.
Budget Deficit.expert: Post-SCOTUS IEEPA ruling (Feb 20), the US tariff revenue base shifted to Section 232 + Section 122 (temporary 10%) + pre-existing Section 301 China tariffs; TPC estimates total tariff revenue of $194bn in 2026, but the OBBBA's multi-trillion dollar cost and rising debt service (10-year Treasury ~4.2%) are widening the structural primary deficit, constraining the Fed's ability to QE in a crisis without fiscal dominance concerns.

Current Account.beginner: The US buys far more from the rest of the world than it sells, creating a large trade deficit that tariffs were supposed to reduce, but the deficit has not meaningfully narrowed despite record tariff revenues.
Current Account.moderate: The US current account deficit has remained stubbornly wide despite tariff-driven import compression; the Tax Foundation estimates tariffs have 'not meaningfully altered the trade deficit' as dollar strength offsets competitiveness gains; the Iran oil shock could temporarily widen the energy trade deficit before domestic production responds.
Current Account.expert: The persistence of the US current account deficit despite historically high tariff rates confirms the Lerner symmetry theorem in practice: tariffs on imports are offset by equivalent tariffs on exports via currency adjustment and income effects; the structural determinant is the gap between domestic saving and investment, a gap that OBBBA fiscal expansion is actively widening by reducing national saving.

Policy Rate.beginner: The Federal Reserve has kept interest rates at 4.25-4.5%, pausing its rate cuts from last year, as it waits to see whether prices keep falling toward its 2% target, which is now more uncertain because of the oil price spike.
Policy Rate.moderate: The FOMC has been on hold at 4.25-4.5% since late 2025; markets that had priced June cuts before the Iran shock have now pushed the first cut expectation to July-September; FOMC members face a classic stagflation dilemma and NY Fed's Williams has explicitly said tariff-driven inflation has 'temporarily stalled' progress toward the 2% target.
Policy Rate.expert: The FOMC's reaction function is now constrained on multiple dimensions: the dual tariff-and-energy supply shock argues against rate cuts (inflation upside risk), while a cooling labour market and deteriorating business confidence argue for easing; the December dot plot (two cuts in 2026) is now likely inoperative, and any shift toward the 'stagflation hold' scenario would materially re-price the front end of the US rates curve with knock-on effects on EM capital flows and USD strength.

beginner: Canada's economy grew just 1.7% last year, which is barely half the pace most developed countries achieved, meaning the USMCA tariff threat could push growth negative if trade with the US contracts.

Growth this weak leaves little room for error when the Trump administration starts renegotiating USMCA terms, because any hit to trade with Mexico or China exports through Canada would crimp an already fragile expansion.
At 1.7%, Canada's growth is slower than its own long-term trend and slower than the US, so the economy has no cushion to absorb tariff shocks without entering recession territory.
moderate: Canada's 1.7% growth trails the US by more than 2 percentage points this cycle, and the USMCA renegotiation risk means the growth story hinges entirely on whether Trump follows through with tariffs on Chinese goods flowing through Mexico and Canada.
The economy expanded at a 2.1% trend rate from 2015 to 2019, so today's 1.7% signals structural weakness before tariffs even hit, leaving almost no margin for a trade shock.

A 1.7% growth rate with the Bank of Canada cutting rates to 2.25% tells you the central bank expects weakness ahead, not a rebound, so tariff escalation would vindicate the bears betting on a hard landing.
expert: Real GDP expanded 1.7% annualized into Q1 2026 while the BoC cut 200bps from its peak, signaling the bank prices in demand destruction from either trade policy or elevated debt servicing costs on households and firms.

Growth at 1.7% sits 40bps below the estimated 2.1% potential output, meaning negative output gap persists despite rate cuts, so any tariff-driven export contraction would push Canada into technical recession by Q3 2026.

The USMCA renegotiation creates a hard downside tail risk: if Trump implements China tariffs on goods transiting Canada, merchandise export volumes could contract 3 to 5 percent, shaving 0.4 to 0.7 percentage points from headline growth in 2026.

beginner: Canada's inflation fell to 2%, right at the Bank of Canada's target, so the central bank has room to keep cutting rates without fear of reigniting price pressure.

At 2%, inflation is so low and stable that the real risk now is deflation if tariffs disrupt supply chains or if weak growth leads firms to cut prices to survive, which would force the BoC to cut even faster.

Inflation being at target is the good news, but it also means there's no inflation buffer to cushion the economy if tariffs cause a shock, because the BoC can only respond by cutting rates, not by letting prices rise.
moderate: Canada hit the BoC's 2% target as the central bank cut its policy rate 200bps from peak, but the Middle East conflict and dollar strength cited in context could reignite import costs if oil spikes or the CAD weakens further.

At 2%, Canadian inflation is 60bps below the US and 30bps below the developed market average, reflecting both weak demand and the strong US dollar dampening import prices, so tariffs that bypass Canada would actually lift inflation by forcing sourcing away from cheaper imports.

Core inflation tracking at or below headline suggests no underlying price momentum, so the BoC's 2.25% policy rate is already accommodative relative to the inflation backdrop, leaving little room to ease further without pushing real rates into deeply negative territory.
expert: CPI holding at 2.0% with the BoC at 2.25% nominal policy rate implies a 25bps real rate, and with headline inflation tracking sticky services demand, the distribution of risks is now skewed toward disinflation if tariffs or weak growth drive demand destruction.

A 2% CPI print masks goods deflation of approximately 1.2% offset by services inflation near 3.1%, so tariff pass-through on imported goods would initially be muted but would accelerate if firms rebuild margins on tariff-induced cost basis shifting.

The 60bps gap between Canadian and US CPI reflects exchange rate transmission lag, and if the CAD weakens further from 0.72 USD, import deflation reverses and Canada's inflation could spike 50 to 80bps within two quarters, forcing the BoC to pause rate cuts by late 2026.

beginner: Canada's unemployment rate jumped to 6.5%, the highest level in years, meaning one in 15 working-age Canadians can't find a job and the economy is shedding positions instead of creating them.

At 6.5%, unemployment is signaling that growth of 1.7% is not strong enough to absorb new entrants into the workforce, so any tariff shock would push the jobless rate above 7% and trigger a wave of layoffs.

The 6.5% rate is bad news for workers but it explains why the BoC keeps cutting rates, because the central bank cares more about jobs than inflation right now, and it's trying to stimulate hiring before tariffs make things worse.
moderate: Canada's 6.5% unemployment rate has risen 100bps in the past two quarters, outpacing the US jobless rate of 4.2%, which reflects both slower growth and immigration-driven labor supply outstripping job creation in sectors like hospitality and retail.

At 6.5%, the unemployment rate is 1.2 percentage points above the BoC's estimated NAIRU, signaling slack in the labor market that gives the central bank cover to cut rates further even as inflation sits at target.

The gap between Canadian and US unemployment widened as the Trump dollar rally and Middle East uncertainty hit commodity exporters like Canada disproportionately, so tariff escalation could push Canadian joblessness another 80 to 120bps higher than the US over the next 12 months.
expert: The unemployment rate spiked to 6.5% from 5.8% in the past 18 months while participation held flat, indicating demand-side weakness not supply adjustment, and the BoC's cumulative 200bps of cuts have failed to arrest deterioration, signaling structural headwinds beyond cyclical slack.

At 6.5%, Canada's unemployment sits 230bps above the estimated natural rate of 4.2%, so output gap is negative and widening, which means tariff-induced demand destruction could push unemployment to 7.5% by Q4 2026 if goods-export exposure contracts meaningfully.

Youth unemployment in Canada running above 15% and prime-age unemployment at 5.8% suggests polarization in labor market outcomes, so USMCA tariffs hitting manufacturing would disproportionately squeeze workers aged 25 to 44 in Ontario and Quebec, deepening regional inequality.

beginner: Canada's budget deficit widened to 1.5% of GDP, meaning the government is spending $1.50 for every $100 of economic output more than it collects in taxes, which is unsustainable if growth stays at 1.7%.

The deficit grew as weak growth crushed tax revenues while the government resisted spending cuts, so any recession from tariffs would blow the deficit above 2.5% of GDP and force painful choices between austerity or higher debt.

A 1.5% deficit sounds manageable, but it's occurring when unemployment is 6.5% and inflation is low, meaning the government should be running surpluses to save for downturns instead of borrowing to smooth current spending.
moderate: Canada's budget deficit expanded to 1.5% of GDP in 2025 as tax-to-GDP ratios fell and program spending rose, a flip from the 2020 to 2024 period when deficits averaged 0.8% and the government was consolidating.

At 1.5% of GDP, the deficit is the largest since 2021 and reflects both cyclical weakness (lower tax receipts from slow growth) and structural spending commitments (healthcare and housing programs that don't flex with the cycle), so tariffs that trigger recession would blast the deficit to 2.2% or higher.

Canada's debt-to-GDP ratio stands near 85%, so adding 70bps of deficit per percentage point of output loss is dangerous; a 1.5% recession from tariffs would take net debt above 87% and force a credit rating agencies to signal downgrade risk by mid-2027.
expert: The budget deficit widened to 1.5% of GDP in fiscal 2025 from 0.6% in 2023, driven by a 2.1 percentage point decline in the tax-to-GDP ratio and unchanged nominal spending, signaling that the fiscal impulse has turned contractionary relative to trend despite appearing expansionary in percentage-of-output terms.

Net federal debt stands near 43% of GDP and total government debt near 85%, so the deficit at 1.5% of GDP represents a structural deterioration; if tariffs trigger a 1.2 percentage point output loss over 2026 to 2027, the deficit would reach 2.1% of GDP and debt would approach 88%, triggering a Moody's or S&P downgrade watch.

The deficit reflects both demand weakness (cyclical component near 0.7% of GDP) and higher structural spending on transfers and debt servicing (0.8% of GDP), so even if growth rebounds to 2.2% by 2027, the deficit only narrows to 1.1% of GDP, leaving little room for stimulus if tariff impacts materialize.

beginner: Canada's current account deficit hit 0.5% of GDP, meaning the country is borrowing from foreigners to finance consumption and investment, a reversal from the surpluses Canada ran in the early 2010s when commodity exports boomed.

The 0.5% deficit is small but it's growing, and if tariffs disrupt merchandise exports to the US, the deficit would widen to 1.5% of GDP and force the Canadian dollar to weaken further to rebalance trade.

Running a current account deficit means foreign investors own more Canadian assets than Canadians own abroad, so the economy is dependent on capital inflows to fund this gap, and tariff shocks could spook those inflows and crash the currency.
moderate: Canada's current account swung to a 0.5% of GDP deficit from a 0.2% surplus two years ago, driven by a collapse in merchandise trade balances as energy export volumes plateaued and import demand stayed resilient despite weak growth.

The deterioration reflects both cyclical weakness (Canadian growth slower than US growth suppresses exports relative to imports) and structural change (energy commodity prices lower than 2010 to 2014 trends), so tariffs would add another 0.5 to 0.8 percentage point to the deficit by cutting manufacturing and auto exports.

At 0.5% deficit, Canada's external position is weaker than historical norms; the CAD/USD at 0.72 shows the currency has already adjusted significantly, but further depreciation to 0.68 to 0.70 would be needed if the current account deficit expands to 1.2% to 1.5% of GDP.
expert: Canada's current account deteriorated 70bps of GDP in two years to a 0.5% deficit, driven by merchandise trade balance swinging from +0.3% to -0.8% of GDP as goods imports exceeded exports for the first time since 2009.

The deficit reflects weak domestic demand relative to imports and energy export plateau, so if USMCA tariffs reduce merchandise exports by 3 to 4%, the current account deficit expands to 1.1% of GDP, consistent with a CAD/USD floor near 0.68 based on historical current account reversions.

Capital account inflows (FDI plus portfolio flows) have covered the 0.5% deficit so far, but if tariffs trigger recession and capital flight accelerates, the BOP constraint becomes binding and forces the BoC to slow rate cuts or tighten, offsetting growth stimulus and deepening the contraction.

beginner: The Bank of Canada cut its policy rate to 2.25%, down 200 basis points from peak, because growth is weak, unemployment is rising, and inflation is already at target, so the central bank is betting that lower rates will stimulate borrowing and job creation before tariffs hit.

At 2.25%, the policy rate is near historic lows but still 100bps above the 1.25% the BoC cut to during the 2008 crisis, meaning the central bank has ammunition to cut further if a tariff shock triggers a recession.

The aggressive rate-cut path tells you the BoC expects growth to get worse before it gets better, and it's trying to get ahead of the unemployment problem by lowering borrowing costs for households and firms before the tariff hammer falls.
moderate: The BoC cut rates 200bps to 2.25% in the past 18 months, the fastest easing cycle since 2008 to 2009, driven by inflation collapsing to target and growth slowing to 1.7%, yet the economy has not responded with stronger hiring or investment, suggesting secular stagnation rather than cyclical slack.

At 2.25%, the real policy rate sits near 25bps, meaning the BoC is providing near-zero real stimulus, yet household debt service ratios remain elevated at 6.5% of disposable income, so lower rates are not translating to spending because households are deleveraging rather than borrowing.

The policy rate is near the BoC's estimated neutral rate of 2.0% to 2.5%, so the central bank has little room to ease further without moving into deeply negative real territory, which creates a dilemma if tariffs trigger recession and the BoC needs to cut to 1.0% or lower to cushion the blow.
expert: The BoC cut the policy rate 200bps to 2.25% since June 2024 while the Fed cut only 100bps to 4.75%, creating a 250bps gap that should push CAD/USD lower toward 0.68 to 0.70 if the differential widens further, but the currency has stabilized at 0.72, suggesting the market prices in either BoC pause or Fed pivot.

At 2.25%, the BoC's real policy rate of approximately 25bps sits 125bps below the estimated neutral rate, providing significant accommodation, yet core inflation remains sticky at 2.2%, indicating the easing has not yet closed the output gap and unemployment gap continues widening.

Forward guidance suggests the BoC will pause cuts at 2.0% to 2.25% if inflation remains at target, but a tariff-induced demand shock of 0.8 to 1.0% of GDP would force the BoC to cut to 1.25% or lower by Q2 2027, putting the nominal rate at risk of moving below 1% and functional lower bound constraints.

beginner: Canada's stock market gained 4.1% year-to-date in Canadian dollar terms, beating the global average but lagging the US, because investors are hedging their bets on the Canadian economy ahead of the USMCA renegotiation.

The 4.1% gain masks divergence in performance, with financials and energy stocks up 6 to 8% while consumer discretionary and industrials lag, reflecting a market rotated toward defensive plays that profit from rising rates or commodity stability.

A 4.1% gain sounds decent, but in US dollar terms (2.78% YTD) the market has barely kept pace with bonds, signaling that Canadian equity investors see tariff risk as real and are unwilling to extend valuations.
moderate: The TSX gained 4.1% year-to-date in CAD terms while the S&P 500 advanced 8 to 9%, so Canadian equities are underperforming US peers by 400 to 500bps, a gap that reflects both the CAD weakness (down 4% against USD YTD) and investor skepticism toward tariff-exposed sectors like autos, materials, and industrials.

Canadian equity gains were driven by financials (up 6.8% as the Big Five banks repriced lower rate expectations) and energy (up 7.2% as oil steadied near $85/bbl), while tech and consumer stocks lagged as investors rotated away from growth exposure into value and dividends.

The 4.1% gain in CAD or 2.78% in USD means Canadian equities are pricing a recession by mid-2026, because valuations remain depressed (12.5x forward earnings vs. 18x for the S&P 500) and the market is implying flat to down earnings through 2026 to 2027 as tariffs hit exports.
expert: The TSX gained 4.1% YTD in CAD while in USD terms returned only 2.78%, indicating a 130bps currency drag, and the divergence reflects foreign investors hedging CAD exposure due to tariff uncertainty, with options markets pricing a 0.68 to 0.70 USD/CAD floor by year-end 2026.

Canadian equity market breadth shows cyclical underperformance: energy +7.2%, financials +6.8%, but industrials +1.1% and consumer discretionary -0.3%, indicating the market is repricing earnings and valuations lower for tariff-exposed sectors and pricing in BoC rate cuts narrowing bank net interest margins.

Forward P/E ratios for the TSX sit near 12.5x vs. 17.8x for the S&P 500, pricing in Canadian earnings decline of 4 to 6% through 2027 if tariffs hit manufacturing and auto exports, while dividend yields at 3.4% vs. 1.4% for the S&P 500 reflect investor demand for carry to offset capital loss risk.

beginner: Canada's 10-year bond yield is 3.29%, down from 3.7% six months ago, because investors are buying Canadian government debt as a hedge against the tariff threat, driving yields lower and bond prices higher.

At 3.29%, the yield is 80bps higher than the policy rate, so investors are demanding compensation for holding longer-duration risk, but that spread is narrow compared to history, signaling that the market expects the BoC to cut rates further over the next two years.

The falling yield tells you bond investors believe a tariff-induced recession is coming, so they're locking in 3.29% today rather than waiting for yields to fall to 2.5% or lower if the economy contracts and the BoC cuts to 1% or below.
moderate: Canada's 10Y yield fell to 3.29% despite the 10Y US yield holding at 4.25%, creating a 96bps inversion that reflects BoC cuts outpacing Fed easing and investors demanding less term premium on Canadian debt as recession risk rises.

The 3.29% yield sits near the lowest level since 2022 and implies market pricing of two to three more BoC rate cuts (totaling 50 to 75bps) by end of 2026, with the terminal rate near 1.5%, consistent with a recession scenario where unemployment rises above 7%.

Relative to the 2.25% policy rate, the 104bps term premium is tight by historical standards (typically 120 to 150bps), so any tariff shock that accelerates BoC cuts could push the 10Y toward 2.8% to 3.0% if investors shift expectations to 1.0% or lower terminal rate.
expert: The CanGov 10Y yield compressed to 3.29% from 3.74% six months ago, creating a 96bps spread to the US 10Y of 4.25% and a 104bps spread to the BoC's 2.25% policy rate, both tight by historical measures and consistent with market pricing of 75 to 100bps of cumulative BoC cuts through 2027.

The yield curve from 2Y to 10Y steepened to 111bps (mentioned in context) as the market repriced near-term BoC cuts but held longer-term expectations relatively stable, indicating conviction in recession by mid-2026 followed by recovery by 2028.

If tariffs trigger a shock that forces BoC to cut to 0.75% to 1.0% (a 125 to 150bps drop from current levels), the 10Y could fall to 2.4% to 2.7% by Q2 2027, while a soft-landing scenario where BoC stabilizes at 1.75% by 2027 would support the 10Y near 3.1% to 3.3%, implying downside risk dominates from current levels.

beginner: Canada's yield curve steepened to 111bps between the 2Y and 10Y, which is the normal shape and signals that investors expect growth to stabilize over the next five to 10 years even if things get worse in the near term.

A 111bps curve is not as steep as it was during the 2008 crisis (when it reached 200bps) but it's steeper than the inverted curves of 2023, so the market is saying a recession might happen soon but it won't be as bad as 2008.

The steepening tells you that the bond market is positioning for the BoC to cut rates aggressively over the next two years (making 2Y yields fall) while the 10Y holds steady, which is exactly what happens when investors expect a soft landing after a tariff shock.
moderate: The Canadian yield curve steepened to 111bps after inverting in 2023, driven by the BoC cutting 200bps while US 10Y yields held firm, so the curve is now pricing in a recession by mid-2026 (forcing near-term BoC cuts) followed by stabilization (keeping long rates stable).

A 111bps curve compares to the US curve at only 90bps, indicating Canadian investors expect more BoC easing relative to Fed policy than the US curve implies, a view consistent with Canada's worse unemployment (6.5% vs. 4.2%) and slower growth (1.7% vs. 2.8%).

The curve steepness is near its 10-year average of 125bps, so there's room for the curve to flatten if tariffs hit harder than expected and the BoC cuts more than the 50 to 75bps the market currently prices, with the curve potentially falling to 75 to 90bps if unemployment approaches 7.5%.
expert: The 2Y to 10Y Canadian curve steepened to 111bps from an inversion of minus 8bps in June 2023, driven by the 2Y note falling 180bps to 2.10% as BoC cut 200bps, while the 10Y slipped only 45bps to 3.29%, pricing in Fed staying higher for longer relative to BoC terminal rate.

The 111bps steepness is 21bps flatter than the 10-year average (132bps) and 50bps flatter than the pre-GFC average (161bps), indicating the curve is priced for secular stagnation where long-run neutral real rates are structurally lower, not a temporary recession followed by full recovery.

Tariff-induced demand destruction would steepen the curve by 20 to 35bps (via BoC cutting to 1.0% while 10Y falls to 2.8% to 3.0%) only if the market believes tariffs are temporary and growth recovers by 2028; if tariffs are permanent, the curve would flatten and the 10Y could fall below 2.5% as secular growth is repriced lower.

beginner: The Canadian dollar fell to 0.72 USD, the weakest level in two years, because investors are dumping CAD in anticipation of the BoC cutting rates faster than the US Fed and tariffs hitting Canadian exports to the US.

At 0.72, the loonie has lost 5 cents against the US dollar in the past six months, wiping out 6% of purchasing power for Canadian importers and making US goods and travel more expensive for Canadian households.

The weak currency is a double-edged sword for Canada: it helps exporters by making Canadian goods cheaper for foreign buyers, but it hurts consumers because imports cost more, so the tariff threat to exporters combined with a weak CAD means Canadians lose on both fronts.
moderate: The CAD/USD fell to 0.72 from 0.76 eighteen months ago, a 5.3% depreciation driven by the BoC cutting 200bps while the Fed cut only 100bps, creating a 250bps interest rate differential favoring the US dollar and making it expensive to carry CAD.

The weakness reflects both rate differentials and tariff risk premia, with the market pricing the CAD toward 0.68 to 0.70 if USMCA tariffs reduce Canadian export volumes by 2 to 3%, which would force further BoC cuts and widen the rate gap even more.

At 0.72, the CAD is near fair value based on purchasing power parity adjustments for inflation differentials (CAD at 2%, USD at 3%), but the currency has asymmetric downside risk if tariffs trigger a hard landing and capital flows reverse.
expert: The CAD/USD weakened to 0.72 from 0.76 (down 5.3% YTD) driven by a 250bps interest rate differential and tariff uncertainty premium, with options markets pricing a 0.68 to 0.70 floor by year-end 2026 if USMCA tariffs impact Canadian export volumes by 3 to 4%.

At 0.72, the CAD is trading 3 to 4% weaker than the PPP-implied rate of 0.74 to 0.76 adjusted for 2% CPI inflation differential, suggesting the currency is discounting 100 to 150bps of further BoC cuts beyond current market expectations and a hard landing in growth.

CAD weakness benefits energy and materials exporters but hurts automakers and consumer goods importers who now face dual headwinds (tariffs on inputs plus pass-through of currency losses), so a move to 0.68 to 0.70 USD/CAD would trigger a structural reset in North American supply chains that could take 18 to 24 months to resolve.

beginner: Canada's stock market returned only 2.78% in US dollar terms year-to-date, half the gain in Canadian dollar terms, because the weakness in the Canadian dollar from 0.76 to 0.72 against the US greenback wiped out currency gains and exposed the underlying weakness in Canadian stock valuations.

A 2.78% return in USD is barely ahead of inflation and is lagging a simple US Treasury bond yielding 4.3%, meaning Canadian equity investors are taking stock market risk for almost no real return, signaling the market is cheap but not attractive enough to draw US capital.

In USD terms, Canadian equities have delivered less than a bond portfolio for 18 months running, which explains why foreign investors are underweighting Canada and the TSX valuation gap versus the S&P 500 keeps widening.
moderate: The TSX returned 4.1% in CAD but only 2.78% in USD YTD, meaning the CAD/USD currency drag of 130bps consumed one-third of the equity gains, a stark reminder that Canadian equity returns are hostage to the central bank's policy path and tariff dynamics.

At 2.78% in USD, Canadian equities are lagging US equities (S&P 500 up 8 to 9% in USD) by 500 to 620bps, with the gap driven by both valuation compression in exporters (autos, materials) and currency depreciation as the BoC eases relative to the Fed.

The 2.78% USD return reflects market pricing of a 4 to 6% earnings decline for Canadian equities through 2027 if tariffs hit, whereas the S&P 500's 8% gain reflects flat to up earnings guidance; the divergence implies a 400 to 500bps EPS growth gap favoring the US, which will persist if tariff risk materializes.
expert: The TSX gained 4.1% in CAD (2.78% in USD) YTD while the S&P 500 advanced 8.5% in USD, with the 570bps underperformance split between 400bps from lower earnings growth (4 to 6% decline vs. flat in the US) and 130bps from CAD depreciation from 0.76 to 0.72.

In USD terms, the TSX has delivered 2.78% YTD while the 10Y CanGov bond yields 3.29%, implying negative real equity risk premium and explaining why foreign participation in the TSX has declined 15 to 20% in the past six months as capital rotated into fixed income.

If tariffs reduce Canadian export volumes by 3 to 4% and the CAD weakens to 0.68 to 0.70, TSX USD returns could be negative through 2027 as the dual impact of lower earnings (5 to 8% decline) and currency depreciation (additional 2 to 4%) erases both dividend yield and capital appreciation.

beginner: Trump's renegotiation of USMCA could drag Chinese tariffs into Canada and Mexico's trade arrangements, which would raise prices for Canadian importers and consumers.
Canada's inflation is already well-controlled at 1.78%, but new tariffs would push it higher and force the Bank of Canada to reconsider rate cuts it might otherwise pursue.
The real risk is a trade shock that disrupts supply chains and forces manufacturers to pass costs through, reversing the disinflationary gains Canada has built.
moderate: USMCA renegotiation to embed China tariffs creates asymmetric shock risk for Canada: inflation is benign at 1.78%, but tariff extension could force a 50 to 100 bps upside surprise to the 2% full-year forecast within months.

The Bank of Canada holds rates at 2.25%, 0% above forecast equilibrium and well below US rates (3.64%), leaving room to cut if trade pressure doesn't materialize, but tariff news removes that optionality rapidly.

Unemployment sits at 6.74% (January), already 24 bps above the 6.5% forecast, indicating slack in the labor market that should've supported BoC cuts but now faces tariff-driven inflation risk that reverses those cuts.
expert: USMCA China tariff extension would transmit to Canadian CPI through import channel (Mexico re-exports to Canada), and with core inflation already tracking forecast at 1.78%, a 50 to 80 bps shock to H2 2026 prints is a downside risk to the 2% full-year call.

BoC policy rate at 2.25% is 0 bps above forecast, but forward curve had priced in 25 to 50 bps of cuts by Q3 2026, those cuts now face rollback risk if tariff momentum persists and forces inflation expectations higher.

Watch May USMCA signaling and April trade data: if Chinese export values to Canada via Mexico surge pre-tariff implementation, BoC cuts disappear and CAD weakens on policy divergence (Fed hold, BoC pin), widening the carry advantage for USD positioning.

fxRegime.label: Free Float
fxRegime.beginner: The Canadian dollar floats freely. The Bank of Canada doesn't try to fix its value, but the currency tends to move with oil prices since Canada is a major oil exporter. CAD/USD shows how many US dollars one Canadian dollar buys. At 0.74, one Canadian dollar buys 74 US cents - or flipped, you give up about 1.35 Canadian dollars to buy one US dollar.
fxRegime.moderate: Free float since 1970. The Bank of Canada has not intervened since 1998. CAD is classified as a commodity currency given Canada's oil export dependency - crude oil prices explain ~60% of CAD variance. The BoC monitors FX as a transmission channel but doesn't target a level.
fxRegime.expert: Free float; last intervention Sept 1998. CAD behaves as a petrocurrency - crude WTI correlation ~0.6 over rolling 12M. Terms of trade channel dominant. BoC operationally focused on inflation targeting; FX pass-through to CPI estimated at 0.05-0.08 over 4Q. Cross-border portfolio flows and rate differentials vs Fed are the secondary drivers.

GDP Growth.beginner: Canada's economy has been growing slowly, hurt by uncertainty over US trade policy, though the oil price surge from the Iran conflict is providing a welcome boost to the country's large energy sector.
GDP Growth.moderate: Canadian GDP growth is tracking below potential as tariff uncertainty dampens business investment and the labour market softens; the oil price surge is a near-term positive for Alberta's fiscal revenues but Eastern refiners face higher feedstock costs, creating a regional divergence in the economic impact.
GDP Growth.expert: Canada's terms-of-trade improvement from oil above $90 is mechanically positive for GDP (energy sector is ~10% of the economy), but the structural headwind from US tariff uncertainty — which has suppressed non-energy business investment — is not alleviated by the oil shock and may intensify if Trump uses the Iran crisis as leverage in bilateral trade negotiations.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: Canadian inflation had been coming down steadily, giving the Bank of Canada room to cut interest rates, but higher fuel prices from the Iran conflict could push prices up again and slow the rate-cutting cycle.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: Bank of Canada CPI was tracking toward target before the Iran shock; the energy price spike directly affects Canadian consumers through gasoline and home heating costs, and indirectly through transportation costs — but Canada's position as a net oil exporter means terms-of-trade effects partially insulate the macro from pure imported inflation.
Inflation (CPI).expert: Canada's inflation dynamics under the Iran shock are asymmetric by region: Alberta and Saskatchewan (net energy exporters) see income gains that are inflationary from the demand side, while Ontario and Quebec (net energy consumers) face a cost-push inflation impulse; the BoC's national CPI target masks these regional divergences, complicating the optimal monetary policy response.

Unemployment.beginner: Canada's unemployment rate has been rising as US tariff uncertainty slows hiring, and businesses are less willing to invest and expand when they are not sure what trade rules will apply in the coming months.
Unemployment.moderate: Canadian unemployment has risen from cycle lows as tariff uncertainty suppressed business investment and hiring in trade-exposed manufacturing sectors; the energy sector boost from oil prices could partially offset this in Alberta, but national unemployment is likely to remain elevated above pre-tariff-war levels through 2026.
Unemployment.expert: Canada's labour market sensitivity to US tariff uncertainty is greater than headline figures suggest: manufacturing sector employment (particularly auto sector supply chains integrated with US production) has contracted, while resource sector employment may partially recover with higher oil prices; the net effect depends on whether the energy sector can absorb workers from manufacturing — a geographic mismatch that constrains the adjustment.

Budget Deficit.beginner: Canada's government budget is relatively well-managed compared to the US, with a deficit of around 1% of GDP, giving the government more flexibility to use spending to support the economy if needed.
Budget Deficit.moderate: Canada's federal deficit (~1% of GDP) provides significant fiscal space relative to G7 peers; higher oil royalties and corporate taxes from the energy price boom could further improve the fiscal position, giving Ottawa flexibility to deploy targeted energy subsidies or income support without threatening fiscal credibility.
Budget Deficit.expert: Canada's fiscal position is structurally stronger than most G7 peers (deficit ~1% of GDP, debt ~40% of GDP), providing meaningful countercyclical capacity; the oil revenue windfall at $90+ WTI generates incremental Alberta Heritage Fund contributions and federal corporate tax revenue that could partially offset potential recession-related social spending increases if tariff-war growth headwinds intensify.

Current Account.beginner: Canada sells more to the rest of the world than it buys, partly thanks to strong oil and agricultural exports — and the oil price surge is making Canada's export revenues even larger this week.
Current Account.moderate: Canada's current account is moving toward a larger surplus as oil export revenues surge; the terms-of-trade improvement from higher crude prices mechanically widens the goods trade surplus, partially offsetting the services deficit; this provides support for the Canadian dollar even as US policy uncertainty creates headwinds.
Current Account.expert: Canada's current account dynamics under the Iran shock are determined by the WCS-WTI spread and pipeline export capacity: at WTI $90, Canadian crude revenues are at their highest in years; Hormuz disruption that strands Middle East barrels could redirect global buyers to Canadian/Permian Basin supply, potentially compressing the WCS discount and amplifying Canadian current account improvement.

Policy Rate.beginner: The Bank of Canada has been cutting interest rates to support a slowing economy, and with inflation coming under control, more cuts were expected — but higher oil prices could now slow or pause this process.
Policy Rate.moderate: The Bank of Canada has been more aggressive than the Fed in cutting rates to support a tariff-dampened economy; the Iran energy shock creates a classic external supply shock dilemma — the BoC wants to ease to support domestic demand but cannot ignore energy-driven CPI upside; the outcome depends critically on the duration of the Hormuz closure.
Policy Rate.expert: The BoC's policy rate trajectory has diverged meaningfully from the Fed's, creating a CAD/USD rate differential that has been a key driver of recent CAD weakness; the Iran shock adds complexity: higher oil prices improve Canada's macro fundamentals (supporting CAD), but global risk-off sentiment and potential synchronised growth slowdown argue for further easing — a divergent signal that complicates BoC communication.

beginner: The UK economy grew just 1.5% last year while most developed nations grew faster, meaning British households are getting richer much more slowly than their peers abroad.
After shrinking for two months late last year, the economy needs to prove it can sustain growth without another stumble, and the next monthly data releases will show if that's actually happening.
Growth this weak leaves little room for the Bank of England to cut rates aggressively without risking another downturn, so interest rate relief for borrowers will come slowly if at all.
moderate: At 1.5%, UK growth trails the US (2.7%) and eurozone (1.0%) by a meaningful margin, exposing why Sterling remains under pressure despite the Bank of England holding rates higher for longer than peers.

The two-month contraction through November followed by a weak recovery suggests the economy lacks momentum heading into spring, when historically consumer spending and business investment should strengthen.
Sub-trend growth this persistently weak forces the Bank of England into a bind: cutting rates risks inflation overshooting their 2.5% target, but holding too long risks tipping into recession again.
expert: Q4 2025 growth of 1.5% annualized reflects a stalled recovery from the November-December contraction, with the 72bps positive yield curve suggesting bond markets doubt rate cuts come soon despite weak real activity.

The 140bps spread between UK growth (1.5%) and US growth (2.7%) persists even as the Bank of England's 3.25% policy rate exceeds the Fed's 4.25-4.50% range, signaling structural weakness rather than temporary cyclical lag.

Watch Q1 2026 monthly GDP prints for any acceleration above 0.3% quarterly pace; failure to reach that threshold makes a 50bps rate cut by summer probable, which would weaken Sterling further against a resilient dollar.

beginner: UK inflation sits at 2.5%, right on the Bank of England's target, which means the central bank has actually won its inflation fight and can now focus on growth instead of fighting price rises.
With inflation stable and low, real wages are finally growing again after years of people getting poorer despite larger paychecks, so household spending could pick up in coming months.
The Bank of England has room to cut interest rates without worrying inflation will spike back up, but weak growth means they have to be cautious or they risk making things worse.
moderate: At 2.5%, UK inflation has cooled fast from the 11% peak in late 2022, now running level with the 2.5% US rate while the eurozone sits at 2.4%, removing the urgency that kept the Bank of England's rates so high.

Energy prices stabilized and wage growth moderated in Q4 2025, the two key drivers that pushed inflation this high initially, meaning further disinflation pressures are weak and the 2.5% level is likely a floor rather than a stepping stone downward.

With inflation no longer a policy headache, the Bank of England's March rate decision will turn entirely on growth weakness, and the 72bps positive yield curve reflects market pricing for a cut by summer despite near-target inflation.
expert: CPI at 2.5% matches the target precisely but reflects base effects from energy price declines fading by April, suggesting Q2 prints will test whether underlying momentum justifies the Bank of England's hawkish hold.

Core inflation tracking slightly above headline (around 3.1%) indicates services price stickiness persists despite 5% unemployment, implying wage-price spiral risks remain non-trivial if growth rebounds sharply and labor markets tighten.

A 72bps positive yield curve coexisting with 2.5% inflation priced near-term disinflation risk; if April-May data shows any acceleration above 2.8%, the Bank of England will abandon rate cut plans and Sterling will rally sharply versus current 1.34 USD valuation.

beginner: The jobless rate sits at 5%, meaning roughly one in twenty people looking for work cannot find a job, and that's high enough that workers have less bargaining power for raises.
Unemployment has been stable at this level for months, not climbing despite weak growth, which usually means employers are reluctant to hire but also not firing anyone yet.
With 5% unemployment and weak economic growth, wage pressure should ease further, giving the Bank of England more confidence to cut interest rates without fueling inflation again.
moderate: At 5%, UK unemployment sits above the pre-pandemic natural rate of 3.8-4%, suggesting meaningful labor market slack that will take quarters to absorb even if growth accelerates to 2% annually.

The stability of unemployment despite back-to-back monthly GDP declines in late 2025 reflects widespread job retention schemes and reluctance by UK firms to lay off workers, mirroring patterns from the 2008 financial crisis.

With 5% unemployment and wage growth moderating to 3-3.5% annually (from peaks above 6%), real wage growth has finally turned positive, but nominal wage growth remains too high to support sub-2.5% inflation if demand recovers quickly.
expert: The 5% unemployment rate masks compositional shifts: youth joblessness runs near 13% while over-25s sit at 4.2%, indicating policy-constrained labor supply among prime-age workers via inactivity rather than true slack.

With unemployment at 5% and the Bank of England holding at 3.25%, the implied NAIRU (non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment) appears to have risen from historical 4% to 4.5-4.8%, reducing the growth headroom before wage-price spiral risks emerge.

Watch April-May employment data for redundancy announcements across financial services and public sector, where layoff cycles typically lead broader weakness by 6-8 weeks; if redundancies exceed 50K per month, unemployment will rise to 5.3-5.4% by Q3 2026, forcing the Bank of England to cut 100bps by year-end.

beginner: The UK government is spending 4% more than it takes in from taxes each year, which means it has to borrow a lot of money just to fund day-to-day operations, not just new investments.
This deficit is high enough to push up government debt levels every single year, and if it stays at 4% forever, eventually lenders will demand much higher interest rates to keep buying UK bonds.
Weak growth makes this worse because companies and workers pay less in taxes while the government still has to spend on unemployment benefits and support for struggling households.
moderate: At 4% of GDP, the budget deficit has widened significantly from the 2.5% recorded in 2022, driven by higher public sector wages (3-3.5% annual raises) and reluctance to cut spending despite weak growth.

The 4% deficit occurs while unemployment sits at 5% and growth crawls at 1.5%, meaning the fiscal position is actually more fragile than the headline number suggests, because cyclical revenues will weaken further if recession hits.

A 4% deficit with 72bps positive yield curve and 4.43% 10Y gilt yields signals bond markets tolerate this level temporarily, but gilts would sell off sharply if the deficit widened to 4.5%+ or if growth fell below 0.5% annualized.
expert: The 4% budget deficit represents a 150bps structural deterioration from 2022 baseline, reflecting operating spending growth of 2.2% annually against revenues growing only 0.8%, unsustainable at current borrowing costs and growth rates.

With gilt yields at 4.43% and the Bank of England holding at 3.25%, real gilt yields have compressed to 193bps, pricing near-zero real growth expectations; a 4% deficit at zero real growth is technically unstable and triggers medium-term fiscal consolidation.

Forward guidance signals spring 2026 fiscal measures; if the Office of Budget Responsibility projects the 4% deficit persisting through 2027-28, gilt yields will spike 30-50bps immediately, forcing fiscal tightening that cuts growth by another 0.3-0.5% annualized and pushes unemployment toward 5.5%.

beginner: The UK buys 2.5% more goods and services from abroad than it sells overseas each year, meaning Britain is borrowing from foreign investors just to fund normal imports.

This deficit happens partly because UK companies don't export enough, but also because foreign companies find it cheaper to sell to Britain than domestic producers can match, a sign the economy isn't competitive enough.

If the current account deficit stays this large for years, eventually foreign investors will demand higher returns to keep financing it, which will weaken Sterling and make imports more expensive for British households.
moderate: The 2.5% current account deficit widened from 1.8% in 2022, driven primarily by a goods deficit that has deteriorated as UK manufacturing has shrunk and import penetration has risen across consumer and capital goods.

Sterling at 1.34 USD should theoretically narrow this deficit by making UK exports cheaper and imports more expensive, but the deficit persists because UK supply capacity has eroded faster than exchange rate movements can fix it.

A 2.5% current account deficit combined with a 4% budget deficit totals a 6.5% twin deficit, historically warning of currency pressure; GBP weakness reflects this arithmetic, and further depreciation toward 1.25-1.28 USD would be necessary to stabilize the current account.
expert: The 2.5% current account deficit breaks into a 3.8% goods deficit partially offset by a 1.3% services surplus, the latter reflecting London's financial center premium that masks underlying competitiveness collapse in tradable goods output.

Current account equilibrium requires either a 200-250bps depreciation of Sterling (to ~1.15 USD) or a 0.8-1.0% real wage decline to make British labor cost-competitive again; neither is politically feasible, so the deficit will persist at 2-3% for 5+ years.

If the Bank of England cuts rates to 2.5% by Q3 2026 while the Fed holds at 4%, the UIP differential narrows to 150bps and Sterling gravitates toward 1.28-1.30 USD; at that level, the current account deficit would widen slightly to 2.7-2.8% before mean-reverting to long-term 2% through compositional shifts in trade.

beginner: The Bank of England's interest rate is 3.25%, which is what banks charge each other for overnight loans, and this ripples through to the mortgage rates and savings rates ordinary people get.
This rate has been on hold for months even though inflation is at the target of 2.5%, because growth is too weak and the Bank of England is worried about triggering a recession if they cut too fast.

Most people expect the Bank of England to start cutting rates later this year as growth remains sluggish, which would lower mortgage payments for some borrowers but also mean savings accounts pay less.
moderate: At 3.25%, the Bank of England's rate sits 100bps above the Fed's 4.25-4.50% range despite inflation being identical at 2.5%, signaling the Bank is hawkish on growth risks while the Fed remains hawkish on inflation (even if inflation has cooled).

The 72bps positive yield curve and near-zero real short-term rates (3.25% minus 2.5% inflation) suggest the Bank of England has already reached peak rates, and market pricing now shows 50bps of cuts by end-2026.

The Bank of England's March 2026 hold despite 1.5% growth and a contraction in late 2025 reveals their faith in a spring rebound; if April-May data disappoints, they will move to a cutting cycle by June, initially 25bps.
expert: The 3.25% policy rate generates a 75bps real rate (3.25% minus 2.5% CPI) and a 72bps positive carry versus the 4.43% gilt yield, pricing the Bank of England's view that terminal rates run 2.8-3.0% in a low-growth regime.

Forward implied rates show zero probability of a 3.50% peak and 70% probability of a 2.75% rate by Q4 2026, consistent with the Bank of England conditioning cuts on Q2 growth rolling over below 0.2% quarterly or unemployment rising above 5.2%.

If the Bank of England cuts to 2.75% by Q4 2026 while the Fed holds at 4.0-4.25%, the 125-150bps rate differential will accelerate GBP weakness toward 1.28 USD and trigger gilt underperformance versus Treasuries (pushing 10Y yields toward 4.8-5.0%), assuming UK growth doesn't accelerate to offset.

beginner: British stocks have risen 6.4% so far this year, which is decent but not spectacular, and it reflects optimism that the recession has ended and profit growth will return.
This gain is being driven mainly by big multinational companies in London that earn money overseas in dollars, so they benefit when the pound gets weaker, not from booming sales to British customers.
Stock gains can easily reverse if growth disappoints or bond yields rise, because much of the upside is priced into valuations already, and the cushion isn't huge.
moderate: UK equities at +6.4% YTD lag the S&P 500 (implied ~8-9% from USD returns), driven primarily by FTSE 100 strength on commodity and financial sector exposure that hedges domestic growth weakness.

The FTSE 100's outperformance masks FTSE 250 (domestic-focused mid-caps) underperformance of 2-3% YTD, revealing that market gains concentrate in large-cap offshore earners insulated from UK recession risk.

Valuations remain compressed at 12-13x forward earnings, below the US at 18-19x, suggesting either the market prices persistent UK weakness or offers value; the answer hinges on whether the Bank of England cuts rates decisively by June.
expert: FTSE 100 gains of 6.4% YTD reflect 65% of returns from currency hedging (Sterling weakness from 1.40 to 1.34 USD) and 35% from earnings recovery, with little multiple expansion as the 72bps positive yield curve pressures risk appetite.

The 6.4% return in GBP versus 5.25% in USD terms indicates foreign investor repatriation and domestic fund rotation out of gilts into equities, unsustainable if gilt yields rise above 4.6-4.7% or if growth revisions turn negative.

Forward signals suggest equity downside to 5-8% annual returns if the Bank of England cuts rates only 75bps by end-2026, but if cuts accelerate to 125bps (signaling recession fears), the FTSE 100 compresses to 10-11x earnings and realizes -8 to -12% drawdown from current levels before stabilizing.

beginner: UK government 10-year bonds pay 4.43% in interest, which is lower than a few months ago but still high enough that the government's debt costs are eating up more tax money.
This yield sits above US equivalents because investors think the UK has more risk, either from politics or from the economy being fragile, so they demand extra return to hold British bonds.

If growth disappoints or the Bank of England starts cutting rates faster than expected, these yields will fall and the value of existing bonds will rise, but if growth surprises, yields could jump to 4.8-5.0%.
moderate: The 4.43% gilt yield exceeds equivalent US Treasuries by 45-50bps, pricing an additional UK risk premium driven by the 4% budget deficit, 2.5% current account deficit, and weak growth momentum.

Gilt yields have compressed from 4.8% highs in late 2024 as inflation cooled and the Bank of England signaled a cutting cycle, but the positive 72bps yield curve indicates the curve is steep by historical standards, suggesting long-term growth expectations are weak.

The 4.43% yield implies a terminal gilt rate near 3.5-3.7% (assuming 0.7-0.8% long-run real rate premium), consistent with the Bank of England cutting to 2.75-3.0%; if gilt yields spike above 4.7%, it signals market doubt about fiscal consolidation or growth recovery.
expert: The 4.43% yield on gilts reflects decomposition of 2.5% expected inflation plus 190bps real rate, where the real rate premium incorporates 140bps of policy rate cuts already priced (from 3.25% to 1.85-2.0%) over 18-24 months.

The 72bps steepness of the curve (4.43% 10Y less 3.71% 2Y rates) signals the market prices a 150-175bps rate cut cycle, compressed from the usual 250bps terminal decline, reflecting skepticism about the Bank of England's ability to support growth without fiscal deterioration.

Watch for gilt yield volatility in Q2 2026 when the Office of Budget Responsibility updates fiscal projections; if the structural deficit is revised above 4.2%, gilts will sell off 30-40bps immediately and the 72bps curve flattens to 40-50bps, signaling a growth recession and accelerated Bank of England cutting to offset.

beginner: The difference between short-term and long-term British interest rates is 72 basis points (0.72%), which is a normal upward slope and means the market expects the Bank of England to keep cutting over the next few years.

An upward yield curve is the healthy normal state, because long-term bond investors want extra return for locking in their money for longer, but when curves invert or flatten sharply, it often signals a coming recession.
This particular curve at 72bps is steeper than it was a year ago, which usually means the market expects weak growth and aggressive rate cuts, not strong growth.
moderate: The 72bps positive yield curve (4.43% 10Y minus 3.71% 2Y) has steepened from 45bps in Q4 2025, as near-term rates have held while long-term rates fell on recession fears and the Bank of England's expected cutting cycle.

A 72bps curve is steep by UK standards (typically 35-50bps in normal growth), signaling market conviction that the Bank of England will cut 150-175bps by 2028, abandoning neutral policy far sooner than economic fundamentals warrant.

If growth reverts toward 2% annualized in Q2-Q3 and the Bank of England signals a shallower cutting cycle (50bps total, not 150bps), the curve will flatten back to 40-50bps as long-term yields rise toward 4.8-5.0%.
expert: The 72bps steepness decomposes to terminal rate expectations of 2.0-2.2% (implied from 10Y real rate of 190bps and 2.5% inflation anchor) versus current 3.25%, pricing 120-125bps of easing by 2028.

The steep curve coexists with a positive 72bps gilt-US Treasury spread, an unusual combination indicating the market expects the Bank of England to outpace Fed cuts due to UK growth weakness, not due to superior UK inflation or asset valuations.

Curve flattening to 40-50bps would occur if April-May 2026 growth data accelerates to 0.4%+ quarterly, prompting the Bank of England to abandon Q2 cuts and hold through summer; conversely, if growth rolls over to 0.1% quarterly, the curve steepens to 100+ bps and 10Y yields fall to 4.0-4.1%.

beginner: The pound trades at 1.34 US dollars, down from around 1.40 a few months ago, which means British travelers to America face higher costs but British exports become cheaper for foreign buyers.

The pound is weaker because the UK economy is growing slower than the US, interest rates aren't supporting the currency the way they used to, and foreign investors worry about the UK's large deficits.
If the Bank of England cuts rates faster than expected, the pound could fall toward 1.25-1.28, but if growth surprises to the upside, it could climb back toward 1.38-1.40.
